sections.title: The Prohibition of a Berakha Le-vatala (Blessing in Vain)
sections.html:
A person is permitted to pray and to praise God in any language he wishes and at any time he wishes, and within prayers and praises it is permitted to mention His holy names, but it is forbidden to recite a berakha le-vatala (a blessing in vain). What is a berakha le-vatala? When one recites a blessing where it does not belong. For example, one who recites Ha-motzi without eating bread, or one who recites Birkat Ha-mazon without having eaten bread beforehand. Likewise, if one recited Ha-motzi and began eating bread, and then recited Ha-motzi again, since he already fulfilled his obligation with the first blessing, the second blessing is in vain. Likewise, one who ate bread and recited Birkat Ha-mazon, if he recites Birkat Ha-mazon again, his blessing will be in vain.

And although in practice, when he recited a blessing in vain he said words of praise and thanksgiving to God, since the Sages instituted that the blessing be recited under specific conditions and he recited it where it does not belong, he has transgressed a rabbinic prohibition. The matter is similar to one who swears a 'shevu'at shav' (a vain oath), for example, one who swears that the heavens are the heavens: although he did not utter a falsehood, since he used the language of an oath for a well-known matter about which there is no need to swear, he has transgressed a Torah prohibition, as it is stated (Shemot 20:6): "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain." Likewise, one who recites a blessing at a time when he does not need to recite it has nullified the purpose of the blessing, for the Sages instituted the recitation of the sanctified text of the blessing in the place where a person needs to thank his Creator and bless Him, and he has disregarded their enactment and recited the blessing in vain. However, since the enactment of the blessings is rabbinic, one who recites them where they do not belong transgresses a rabbinic prohibition. And there is an opinion that one who recites a berakha le-vatala transgresses a Torah prohibition.1

If one erred and recited a blessing in vain, he should immediately say: "Barukh shem kevod malkhuto le-olam va-ed" ("Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever"). There is a certain rectification in this, for by blessing the name of His glorious kingdom, he somewhat dispels the desecration of God's name that he caused when he recited a blessing in vain. And if he said "Barukh Ata Hashem" ("Blessed are You, Lord") and remembered that he does not need to recite a blessing, he should conclude "lamdeni ḥukekha" ("teach me Your statutes"), and thus it turns out that he recited a complete verse from Tehillim (119:12), and he has not committed the prohibition of a berakha le-vatala (SA 206:6).

sections.title: An Unnecessary Blessing
sections.html:
In addition to the prohibition of reciting a berakha le-vatala, there is also a prohibition of causing an unnecessary blessing (berakha she-eina tzerikha). For example, one who wishes to eat an apple and a pear, since the blessing of both is the same, must recite one blessing before eating them and one after eating them. If, after he finishes eating the apple, he recites Borei Nefashot so that he will thereby need to recite Ha-etz and Borei Nefashot again on the pear, it turns out that he has caused himself to add two blessings. It is forbidden to do this, because a blessing is a precious and sanctified thing; when it is said for a need it adds blessing, and when it is said without need, its value is impaired.

However, this prohibition is less severe, and therefore when a person has a doubt in matters of blessings, and by causing an additional blessing he will resolve the doubt, he is permitted to cause an additional blessing. For example, when it is clear that a certain food is secondary (tafel) to another, one recites the blessing on the primary food (ikar) and exempts the secondary one, and if he recites a blessing on the secondary food separately and on the primary food separately, he transgresses the prohibition, for he causes himself to recite an unnecessary blessing. But when there is a doubt whether the food is indeed secondary to the other, it is preferable that he first eat each of the two foods separately, so that he will recite its own blessing over each one. And although by eating each food separately he causes himself to recite an additional blessing, there is no prohibition of an unnecessary blessing in this, since he does so in order to resolve the doubt (above 11:2).

Likewise, it is permitted to cause additional blessings in order to complete one hundred blessings on Shabbat, provided that he does so in a manner that appears natural to the order of his eating. For example, it is permitted to ask that the fruit be brought after the meal, whereby he will gain another blessing. For if he eats them during the meal, he will recite Ha-etz over them at the beginning but will not recite a final blessing over them, since Birkat Ha-mazon will exempt them as well. But if he eats the fruit after the meal, he will recite a blessing over them at the beginning and at the end. There is no prohibition in this, since on a weekday too, people sometimes postpone eating fruit until after the meal. However, on a weekday it is permitted to do this only when one genuinely wishes to make a break between the meal and eating the fruit, whereas on Shabbat it is permitted to do this even when the main aim is to complete one hundred blessings. Likewise, it is permitted to eat mezonot and fruit before the Shabbat meal in order to complete one hundred blessings, provided that he pauses for half an hour, or at least a quarter of an hour, between eating them and the beginning of the meal, for then he does not appear as one who is interested only in adding blessings, but as one who wishes to delight in Shabbat with many tastings (see above 3:12).2

sections.title: In Doubtful Cases of Blessings We Are Lenient
sections.html:
When there is a doubt whether one must recite a certain blessing, there is no obligation to recite it, for we hold the rule that whenever we have a doubt concerning a rabbinic matter, the halakha is lenient (safeka de-rabbanan le-kula). And since the enactment of the blessings is rabbinic, there is no obligation to recite a blessing where there is a doubt. And if one wishes to volunteer and recite the blessing, he enters a doubtful prohibition, for we have learned that it is forbidden to recite a blessing in vain. This is the meaning of the rule "safek berakhot le-hakel" ("in doubtful cases of blessings we are lenient"): when there is a doubt whether one must recite a certain blessing, one should be lenient, and it is forbidden to be stringent and recite the blessing. For example, a person who is in doubt whether he ate a kezayit, the amount that obligates a final blessing, should not recite the blessing.3

Some say that only when the doubt is more or less evenly balanced, for example when close to half of the poskim hold that one should not recite the blessing, is it forbidden to recite it. But if, according to a clear majority of the poskim, one must recite the blessing, one recites it and does not take into account the minority opinion. In contrast, others say that even when only a minority of the poskim hold that one should not recite the blessing, there is still a doubt here, and it is forbidden to recite it. And this is the accepted ruling. That is, the matter of a blessing must be absolute, so that a person stands with certainty before his Creator and blesses; but when he is in doubt, he cannot say a blessing before his Creator.

All this concern for the opinion of poskim who hold that one should not recite a blessing applies only when there is no clear custom; but if there is a custom to recite the blessing, one recites it in accordance with the custom, for the very fact that people were accustomed to recite it shows that this is how the halakha was decided, and there is no longer a doubt in it.4

sections.title: Is It Permitted to Derive Benefit When in Doubt Whether One Recited a Blessing?
sections.html:
If one wished to eat something and was in doubt whether he had already recited a blessing over it, since in doubtful cases of blessings we are lenient, he should eat without a blessing. If it is possible to find a solution, it is proper to do so in order to resolve the doubt. For example, if there is a person there who needs to recite the same blessing, he should ask him to have in mind to fulfill his obligation with his blessing, answer Amen after him, and eat immediately. And regarding foods whose final blessing is Borei Nefashot, if he goes out of his house for a short walk, an interruption will be created, and thus when he returns he will be able to recite a first blessing again over the food he wishes to eat (above 9:7). He is not considered one who caused himself to recite an unnecessary blessing, since he did so in order to resolve the doubt (above, section 2). In any event, when there is no solution, according to the letter of the law it is permitted to eat, for only when there is certainty that one must recite a blessing is it obligatory to recite it, and when there is no certainty, it is not possible to recite it. One who wishes to be stringent with himself should refrain from eating.

Some say that when a person is in doubt whether he must recite a blessing, he may say the blessing, and instead of saying the sanctified Name he should say its Aramaic translation, for example, he should say "Barukh Raḥmana Melekh ha-olam" ("Blessed is the Merciful One, King of the universe") and continue saying the blessing in Hebrew. In this way, on the one hand he will not sin by uttering the name of Heaven in vain, and on the other hand he will fulfill the obligation of the blessing, since even one who recites a blessing in another language fulfills his obligation (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 202:3). Many disagreed with this, holding that the prohibition of a berakha le-vatala does not depend on God's name, but on the very fact that a person intends to utter a blessing when he is not obligated in it. And just as one who swears a vain oath mentioning God's name in a foreign language transgresses a Torah prohibition, so too one who recites a blessing mentioning God's name in a foreign language transgresses the prohibition of a berakha le-vatala (Responsa Rabbi Akiva Eiger, Kamma 25). Since the matter is disputed, it is preferable to refrain from it (Yeḥaveh Da'at 6:15).

Some Aḥaronim recommended that whenever, because of a doubt, it is impossible to recite a blessing, it is good to think the blessing in one's heart. God sees into the heart that he wishes to give thanks before Him, and at the same time there is no concern of a blessing in vain in this (Pri Megadim, Rabbi Akiva Eiger, Ben Ish Ḥai, Matot 14. According to the Rambam one fulfills the obligation through thought, and even according to his view there is no concern of a blessing in vain in this).5

sections.title: One Hundred Blessings
sections.html:
A person is obligated to recite one hundred blessings every day (Menaḥot 43b; SA 46:3). King David instituted this at a time when there was a plague, and one hundred souls of Israel died each day. David understood through the holy spirit (ru'aḥ ha-kodesh) that the plague was caused because people were not blessing God in completeness, with one hundred blessings every day, and he arose and instituted for Israel that they should recite one hundred blessings every day (Bamidbar Rabba 18:21; Tur OḤ 46).

Men are obligated in this mitzva, for they are obligated to pray three prayers a day, and through this, together with the meals, they reach more than one hundred blessings every day. But women are exempt from three prayers every day, and consequently they do not have the possibility of reaching one hundred blessings.

On Shabbatot and Yamim Tovim, when there are fewer blessings in the Amida prayer, one must add several more blessings over various kinds of spices and foods (Menaḥot 43b). When this is not possible, such as on Yom Kippur and other fast days, when all the blessings of enjoyment over food are lacking, one may have in mind to include the blessings one hears from those called up to the Torah and for the Haftara. And when necessary, one may also include the blessings one hears from the ḥazan in the repetition of the Amida (MB 46:14).6

sections.title: Rules Regarding the Wording of Blessings
sections.html:
There are blessings that the Sages instituted in a short form, containing a single expression of thanks without lengthy wording, such as Birkhot Ha-shaḥar and the blessings of enjoyment (birkhot ha-nehenin). And there are blessings that were instituted in a long form, which include many details. In a short blessing one says "Barukh Ata" ("Blessed are You") etc. once, whereas a long blessing opens with "Barukh Ata," and at the conclusion of the blessing one again says "Barukh Ata," as for example in the blessings of Asher Yatzar and Me'ein Shalosh. And when it is a long blessing that is always adjacent to another blessing, it does not open with "Barukh," for the preceding blessing that opens with "Barukh" is considered its opening (Pesaḥim 104b). Therefore, in the blessings of the Amida prayer and of Birkat Ha-mazon, only the first blessing opens with "Barukh," and in all the rest, although they are long, one says "Barukh Ata" only at their conclusion (see above 4:2). And there are a few blessings of thanksgiving which, although they are sometimes said not adjacent to another blessing, do not open with "Barukh," such as the blessing Elohai Neshama that one says in the morning (SA 6:3; and see there MB 12).

One should not change the wording of the blessings instituted by the Sages, and if one changed it, as long as he said the four fundamental elements of every blessing, he has fulfilled his obligation. These are the four fundamental elements: a) "Barukh" ("Blessed"); b) God's name; c) that He is King of the universe;
d) the specific content of the blessing; and there are blessings whose content includes several essential details, as in the blessings of Birkat Ha-mazon (above 4:5). If one omitted one of these elements, he has not fulfilled his obligation (Berakhot 40b; SA 214:1; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 185:2; MB 68:1).

When there is a series of blessings recited in sequence, such as Birkat Ha-mazon, or the blessings of Keriat Shema, or the Shemoneh Esrei prayer, there is no need to mention His kingship in all the blessings, for since one already said this in the first blessing, all the blessings recited afterwards in sequence rely on it. But God's name must be mentioned in all the blessings, because the foundation of a blessing is turning to God, and therefore one must mention His name.

sections.title: Two People Eating Together – Is It Good That One Recite the Blessing?
sections.html:
When two people come to eat bread together, since they have established themselves to eat together, it is good that one recite Ha-motzi and exempt the other. This is because a blessing said on behalf of two people is more important, and it contains a greater expression of thanksgiving to God (Berakhot 42b; see above 5:1). And this is the practice at Shabbat meals: since they have gathered to eat together, the head of the household recites Ha-motzi on behalf of everyone, for "in the multitude of people is the King's glory" (Berakhot 53a; SA 167:11; above 3:4. And see above 1:10 regarding the laws of one who fulfills the obligation on behalf of another).

But if each one is eating for himself, and they are not waiting for one another, it is better that each recite the blessing for himself. And if one does not know how to recite the blessing, even though each of them is eating for himself, the one who knows how to recite the blessing should recite it aloud in order to exempt his companion who does not know how to recite it (see SA 167:13).

Regarding eating fruit and other foods, if they did not establish themselves to eat together, according to all opinions it is proper that each recite the blessing for himself. And if they established themselves to eat together, some say that it is preferable that one recite the blessing aloud and exempt the other (SA 213:1). Others say that only eating bread or drinking wine is considered something that unites the group, and with them it is good that one recite the blessing on behalf of everyone. But other foods and beverages are not so important that people unite to eat or drink them, and therefore even when they sit to eat them together, as long as they are not within the framework of a meal with bread, it is preferable that each recite the blessing for himself (Rema there; MB 11). In practice, since each of the customs has its own advantage, those eating may choose whether to prefer that one recite the blessing for everyone or that each recite the blessing for himself.

Regarding the final blessing, it is agreed that it is preferable that each recite the blessing for himself; but if there is someone there who is concerned that perhaps he does not remember the blessing properly, or who is in doubt whether he ate the amount that obligates a blessing, it is proper that one recite the blessing aloud in order to exempt him (SA 213:1. And see above 5:6 regarding zimun).

sections.title: The Obligation to Answer Amen
sections.html:
One who hears a Jew recite a blessing is obligated to answer "Amen" after him (SA 215:2). And even if he did not hear the entire blessing but only its end, he is obligated to answer Amen (Ḥayei Adam; MB 215:6). And if he did not hear the blessing, but he knows which blessing is being recited, and understood from the movements of the lips of the one reciting it that he finished the blessing, he may answer Amen after him but is not obligated to (Be'ur Halakha there; Rema 124:8).

It is forbidden to answer Amen after one who recites a blessing in vain (SA 215:4). But one who heard a blessing from someone who recites it according to his custom, even though the listener is not accustomed to say this blessing, is obligated to answer Amen to it, since the one who recited it acted properly according to his custom. For example, one who is not accustomed to recite a blessing over Hallel on Rosh Ḥodesh must answer Amen after one who is accustomed to recite it.7

One who hears a blessing from a minor who has reached the age of training (ḥinukh) for blessings, that is, he understands the meaning of the blessing and knows how to say it properly, is obligated to answer Amen after him (SA 215:3). Children generally reach this at the age of five or six. And if a minor who has not yet reached this stage recites a blessing, one does not answer Amen after him, but one praises him for having recited the blessing nicely, in order to accustom him to recite blessings.

When teaching a child to recite a blessing, one accustoms him to say the wording of the blessing with God's name, and there is no prohibition of a berakha le-vatala in this, since he does so for the sake of learning. But one does not answer Amen to a blessing intended for practice (SA 215:3).

One who hears a non-Jew recite a blessing in a place where it is fitting to say it, such as before or after eating, should answer Amen after him, since his intention is for the sake of Heaven. But if there is a concern that he is directing it toward idolatry, even though he says the blessing in our wording, one should not answer Amen after him (SA and Rema 215:2; MB 12). Above, in chapter 1, halakha 9, the mitzva of answering Amen and its great virtue are explained.

sections.title: Does One Fulfill One's Obligation by Hearing Through a Loudspeaker?
sections.html:
The poskim disagree whether one who hears a blessing through a telephone or a loudspeaker fulfills his obligation. Some say that since the sound came forth from the power of the one reciting the blessing, and the listener heard it immediately, even though the sound passed through an electrical device, its law is like the voice of the one reciting the blessing, by hearing which one can fulfill one's obligation. Others say that since the sound heard is not the original voice of the one reciting the blessing, but rather the electrical device picked it up as electrical signals and afterwards converted it again into a new sound, it is like hearing the sound of a machine, through which one does not fulfill one's obligation.

In practice, one should take into account the opinion of the stringent poskim, and not perform mitzvot that depend on hearing by means of electrical devices. However, when there is no choice, it is preferable to perform the mitzva by means of electrical devices than to lose it entirely. For example, one who is in a place where he cannot hear the reading of the Megilla or Havdala should preferably hear it over the telephone or in a live radio broadcast. And in zimun, when there are many people and it is difficult to hear the one leading the zimun without a loudspeaker, it is good to make use of it (in zimun there is more room for leniency, as explained above 5:6, note 10).

The poskim disagree regarding the law of a hard-of-hearing person who uses a hearing aid. Some say that he does not fulfill his obligation, since he does not actually hear with his ear. On the other hand, some say that hearing through the device is like hearing through the ear, since in practice he heard the sound. And some say that for the mitzva of hearing the shofar one must hear the shofar directly without any intermediary, but other mitzvot can be fulfilled by hearing through a device. In practice, for rabbinic mitzvot one may rely on the lenient opinion, and for Torah mitzvot, when possible, it is preferable to hear without the device.

One who hears blessings and Kaddish through a loudspeaker must answer Amen. And one who hears through a telephone or a live radio broadcast should preferably answer Amen, but is not obligated to.8

sections.title: One Who Eats Forbidden Food
sections.html:
One does not recite a blessing over eating a food that is forbidden to be eaten, neither a first blessing nor a final blessing, for how can one thank God for an enjoyment that came into his hands through a transgression? And if he recites a blessing, his blessing will not be praise but rather blasphemy and an affront to the honor of Heaven. There is no difference whether the food is forbidden by Torah law, such as meat that was not slaughtered according to halakha, or forbidden by rabbinic law, such as fruit from which terumot and ma'asrot were not separated at a time when most of Israel is outside the Land; in any case one does not recite a blessing over them (Mishna Berakhot 45a; SA 196:1).

Likewise, one who steals food, in addition to having to return the stolen item, is forbidden to recite a blessing over it, and if he recites a blessing it is not a blessing but blasphemy, as it is stated (Tehillim 10:3): "The robber who blesses has blasphemed the Lord" (based on Sanhedrin 6b).

One who eats kosher food at a time when he is forbidden to eat, for example one who eats on a fast day, or on Motza'ei Shabbat before Havdala, or before the Shaḥarit prayer, or on Sukkot outside the sukka, since the food itself is kosher and only the time or place of eating is improper, must recite a blessing over his enjoyment of the kosher food.

One who is in danger and, in order to save himself, must eat forbidden foods, such as nevelot and tereifot (meat from animals that were not properly slaughtered or that had fatal defects), must recite a blessing over them. And although he would prefer not to need to eat them, since in practice he eats them in a permitted manner, for saving a life overrides all the mitzvot, he must recite a blessing over his enjoyment. However, if he finds the forbidden food repugnant, for example he is forced to eat pork and feels disgust at it, he should not recite a blessing, since in practice he does not enjoy it (SA 196:2; 204:9; MB 204:48).9

sections.title: One Who Recited a Blessing Over Something Forbidden – Should He Eat?
sections.html:
If one erred and recited a blessing over a food that is forbidden to be eaten, such as over tereifa meat, or ḥametz on Pesaḥ, he should not eat any of it, and his blessing was in vain. And even if the prohibition of eating is only rabbinic, he should not taste it at all.

Likewise, if one ate a meat food and within an hour erred and recited a blessing over a dairy food, he should not taste the dairy food, since according to all opinions this is forbidden by rabbinic law. But if, before reciting the blessing over the dairy food, he had managed to eat a pareve food and drink, whereby his mouth was cleansed of remnants of the meat, or an hour had passed since he finished eating the meat, since there are Rishonim who permit eating dairy at that point, he should taste a little of the dairy food, so that his blessing will not be in vain (see Peninei Halakha: Kashrut 26:2, notes 3 and 5).

If one erred on Motza'ei Shabbat before Havdala and recited a blessing over a food, and before he began to eat remembered that it is forbidden to eat before Havdala, he should taste a little of the food. Since there is no prohibition in the food itself, in order that his blessing not turn out to be in vain, it is preferable that he taste a little after his blessing. The same law applies to one who erred and recited a blessing over a food before Kiddush (Rema 271:5; MB 26).

Likewise, if one erred and recited a blessing over something that is not eaten because of a custom, he should taste it, so that his blessing will not be in vain. Therefore, one who mistakenly recites a blessing over meat during the Nine Days should taste a little of the meat. This is because the prohibition of eating meat during the Nine Days is due to custom. Furthermore, there is no joy in a mere taste, and therefore it barely detracts from the mourning.

Likewise, one who erred and recited a blessing over a food before the Shaḥarit prayer should taste a little, because there is no expression of arrogance in this tasting, for he tastes only in order to be saved from a blessing in vain.

If one forgot that it is a fast day and recited Shehakol over water, according to most poskim he should not drink. This is because the prohibition of eating and drinking on a fast day is clear, and one should not take an action and transgress this prohibition.10

sections.title: Giving Food to One Who Will Not Recite a Blessing
sections.html:
When a person offers his friend food, he bears a responsibility to see to it that he recites a blessing, for otherwise it turns out that he assists him in stumbling into the prohibition of eating something without a blessing (SA 169:2).

But if his friend is secular, and there is a reasonable concern that if he asks him to recite a blessing he will be offended, he should offer him food and drink without asking him to recite a blessing. For if he offends him, he will cause him to stumble into a more severe prohibition, for he will cause tension and hatred between them, and he may even cause him to distance himself from Torah and mitzvot. However, one should not be overly concerned that the guest will be offended, since in practice most Jews who are not defined as religious are happy to recite a blessing, or at least to answer Amen, when they are guests of their religious friend or relative. Therefore, it is generally possible to gently suggest to the guest that he recite a blessing, and at the very least the host can recite the blessing aloud, and by the guest answering Amen, he will be considered to some extent a partner in the blessing (see Igrot Moshe OḤ 5:13; Minḥat Shlomo 1:35; Shevet Ha-levi 4:17; Piskei Teshuvot 169:3-4).

sections.title: The Law Regarding One Who Errs in His Blessing
sections.html:
If one took a cup of water in his hand, and while saying "Barukh Ata Hashem Eloheinu Melekh ha-olam" ("Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe") he erred and thought he was holding wine, and intended to recite Ha-gafen, and then remembered that it was water and concluded "she-ha-kol nihya bi-dvaro" ("by whose word all things came to be"), he has fulfilled his obligation (Rashi and Tosafot).

And even if he remembered his error only after he finished the blessing and said "borei pri ha-gafen" ("who creates the fruit of the vine"), and immediately remembered and said, within the time it takes to speak a few words (tokh kedei dibbur), "she-ha-kol nihya bi-dvaro," since in practice he corrected himself, he has fulfilled his obligation. There are some Rishonim who hold that since he erred in the blessing itself, both in his intention and in his speech, he has not fulfilled his obligation (as implied by Rashi and Tosafot). However, because of the doubt, most Rishonim decided that he has fulfilled his obligation (the Ra'avad and the Rosh, based on the Geonim and the Rif; and so too wrote SA 209:2; MB 5-6).

And if he said the entire blessing over the water properly, and after he finished he became confused and thought that he needed to correct the blessing, and again concluded "borei pri ha-gafen": some say that he has not fulfilled his obligation, since he decided to conclude the blessing over wine, and the blessing of Ha-gafen does not exempt water (the Ra'avad and the Razah). Others say that since at first he said the blessing properly, he already fulfilled his obligation, and the fact that afterwards he "corrected" himself cannot invalidate the blessing that had already been concluded properly (the Ramban, based on the Geonim). And since in doubtful cases of blessings we are lenient, he has fulfilled his obligation.11
